sections.title: My Family
sections.content: To say whose someone is, put a possessive in front of the noun: 'mi madre', 'tu familia', 'su hermano'. The important thing — and it is the opposite of English — is that a possessive agrees with the thing owned, not with the owner. One brother is 'mi hermano', two are 'mis hermanos', whether the speaker is a man or a woman.

items.spanish: Hoy vamos a hablar con mi familia por videollamada.
items.english: Today we're going to talk to my family on a video call.

items.spanish: Primero aparece mi madre. Después aparecen mi padre y mi hermano.
items.english: First my mother appears. Then my father and my brother appear.

items.spanish: Nuestro apartamento es pequeño, pero es muy cómodo.
items.english: Our apartment is small, but it's very comfortable.

sections.content: 'Su' does a lot of work — his, her, their, and your when you are being formal. Spanish lets context sort it out, and says 'la madre de Carlos' when it really needs to be clear. Only 'nuestro' and 'vuestro' change for gender: 'nuestro apartamento', 'nuestra profesora'.
